context.concept_name: Relational database and table structure basics

coverage.learning_objective: Recognize that relational data lives in named tables made of rows and columns, and identify what a table's rows and columns represent for a small real-world dataset.

required_facts.statement: A relation, also called a table, holds data where each row (also called a record or tuple) represents one group of related data values.
The columns of a table are also called fields or attributes.
A table has a name distinct from every other table in the database, contains no duplicate rows, and the sequence of its rows and columns is insignificant.
A database is composed of multiple tables, each holding data.
Each table should contain information about one kind of thing only, such as the Branch or the Customer, rather than mixing unrelated things in one table.

teaching_blocks.content: Now that you've worked with a single delivery-orders table in pandas, picture the same business run out of a real database instead of one spreadsheet: a customers table, an orders table, a products table, each living on its own. A relational database is built out of exactly this kind of piece.

A relation -- what SQL calls a table -- holds data where each row (also called a record or tuple) represents one group of related data values, and its columns are also called fields or attributes. So the customers table's rows are individual customers, and its columns (customer_id, name, city) are the attributes recorded about every customer. A database is composed of multiple tables like this, each holding its own kind of data -- customers, orders and products each get their own table rather than being crammed together.

A few properties keep a table well-formed. It has a name distinct from every other table in the database -- 'customers' is not also used for anything else -- and it contains no duplicate rows; the order its rows and columns happen to be listed in is not meaningful. On top of that, each table should contain information about one kind of thing only, such as the Customer or the Order, rather than mixing unrelated things into one table -- which is exactly why a customer's details and an order's details live in two separate tables instead of one merged one.

Reading a relational database, then, starts with the same question every time: which table am I looking at, what one kind of thing does each of its rows represent, and what does each column tell me about that thing. That question is what the SELECT statement you write next will answer.

video_need.reason: This is a static structural definition -- what a table, row and column are, and that a database holds several of them for different entities. A short labeled diagram of the customers/orders/products tables would help, but the text and the multi-table example already make the structure clear without any demonstration.

practice_anchor.objective: Given a small shop scenario (books, customers, loans), choose a table name, its columns, and one example row for each table, keeping one kind of thing per table.
practice_anchor.success: The learner picks a table whose name is not reused, columns that all describe one kind of thing, and an example row that fits those columns, and rejects a design that mixes two kinds of thing or repeats a row.

visual_anchor.purpose: Two small tables (customers and orders) side by side, with a row, a column and each table name visibly labelled using the SQL terms record/tuple and field/attribute.

teaching_notes: Introduce the customers/orders/products schema here -- it is reused across the whole SQL and data-modeling run.
Don't explain SELECT syntax yet -- that's the next concept.

coverage.learning_objective: Write a SELECT statement that retrieves specific, named columns from a table, aliasing them for readability.

required_facts.statement: The SELECT list, between the keywords SELECT and FROM, specifies the expressions that form the output rows of the SELECT statement.
Writing AS output_name after a column's expression in the SELECT list names that output column; AS can be omitted if the desired name does not match a keyword.
The FROM clause derives the table (or tables) that a query reads from.
Writing * in the SELECT list is shorthand for all columns of the selected rows; table_name.* narrows that to one table's columns when a query reads from more than one table.

teaching_blocks.content: You know the customers table has columns customer_id, name and city. To actually pull that data out of the database, you write a SELECT statement.

The SELECT list -- everything between the keywords SELECT and FROM -- specifies the expressions that form the output rows of the statement, and the FROM clause derives the table (or tables) the query reads from. So SELECT name, city FROM customers reads the customers table and returns just those two columns, for every row.

You can also rename an output column by writing AS output_name after its expression in the SELECT list -- AS can be left out if the name you want doesn't collide with a keyword. SELECT name AS customer_name, city FROM customers returns the same data, but the first column is now labeled customer_name in the result instead of name.

Writing * in the SELECT list is shorthand for all columns of the selected rows, so SELECT * FROM customers returns every column of every customer row without listing them one by one; table_name.* narrows that to just one table's columns when a query reads from more than one table.
SELECT ... FROM is the shape every query in this path builds on: FROM says which table to read, and the SELECT list says which columns -- renamed or not -- come back out.

video_need.reason: Watching a SELECT statement actually run against the customers table, and seeing the output columns appear in the chosen order and names, makes the SELECT-list/FROM mapping concrete faster than reading about it -- but the definition and example here are complete enough to stand alone.

media.group_title: SELECT and FROM picking just the columns you need

segments.label: Live demo: writing SELECT first_name, country FROM customers
segments.summary: Starts from the situation where you do not need every column of a table, then builds a query that lists just two columns, first name and country, after SELECT and names the customers table after FROM. The result shows only those two columns and not the others, such as the customer ID or the score. A short on-screen step-through then shows the database going to the table first and then picking the requested columns. No column is renamed anywhere in it.

bridge_note.before: Watch how the column list after SELECT decides exactly which columns come back and the table named after FROM supplies them.
bridge_note.after: The clip never renames a column; AS output_name is taught in the text above. The step-through's FROM-first order previews execution order covered later; for now just note that the database reads the table before picking columns.

context.concept_name: Table and column aliasing for readability

coverage.learning_objective: Give tables and columns temporary alternate names with AS to make queries, especially multi-table queries, more readable.

required_facts.statement: A table alias is a temporary name given to a table reference, written FROM table_reference AS alias, where AS is optional.
Once a table alias is assigned, the table must be referred to by its alias, not its original name, for the rest of that query.
A column can be aliased the same way, by writing AS output_name after the column's expression in the SELECT list.

A column can be referenced as correlation.columnname, where correlation is a table name or a table alias defined in the FROM clause; the correlation name and dot can be omitted if the column name is unique across all the tables used in the query.

teaching_blocks.content: Typing out orders or customers in full every time gets tedious, especially once a query starts referring to a table's columns repeatedly. SQL lets you give a table a short temporary name for the query instead.

A table alias is a temporary name given to a table reference, written FROM table_reference AS alias, with AS optional -- FROM orders AS o gives the orders table the short name o for the rest of that query. Once assigned, the table must be referred to by its alias, not its original name, for the remainder of the query -- writing FROM orders AS o and then referencing orders again later would be an error.

A column can be aliased the same way, by writing AS output_name after the column's expression in the SELECT list, exactly as you already saw with SELECT. A column can also be referenced as correlation.columnname, where correlation is a table name or an alias defined in the FROM clause -- so with orders aliased to o, you can write o.customer_id instead of orders.customer_id. The correlation name and dot can be left off entirely when the column name is unique across every table used in the query.

On a single table like SELECT o.order_id, o.delivery_time_minutes FROM orders AS o, qualifying a column this way is optional. The alias starts to matter once a query reads from more than one table at a time and two of those tables happen to share a column name -- qualifying which table's copy you mean is what keeps the query unambiguous.
Whether it's naming a table or a column, an alias is the same idea: a temporary rename that exists only for the current query, chosen to make the query shorter or its columns clearer to read.

video_need.reason: Aliasing is a renaming convention applied inside a single query -- a short annotated-code example showing FROM orders AS o and o.customer_id is enough; there's no changing state or process to demonstrate.

practice_anchor.objective: Write a single-table query that gives the orders table a short alias, qualifies the columns with that alias, and renames one output column with AS. (The multi-table version of this practice waits for sql.inner_join, which is taught later.)
practice_anchor.success: The query runs, every column reference uses the alias rather than the original table name, and the renamed output column appears under its new label.

coverage.learning_objective: Remove duplicate rows from a query's results using DISTINCT so each unique value or row appears once.

required_facts.statement: SELECT DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the result, keeping one row from each group of duplicates.
SELECT ALL, which is the default when DISTINCT is not written, keeps all rows including duplicates.

teaching_blocks.content: SELECT DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the result, keeping one row from each group of duplicates. SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers returns each city that appears in the customers table exactly once, no matter how many customers share it.

SELECT ALL is the default behavior when DISTINCT is not written -- it keeps every row, duplicates included. So SELECT city FROM customers (no DISTINCT) would list Lagos once per customer who lives there, while SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers lists Lagos only once.

video_need.reason: A before/after row count is easy to state in one sentence and one short example table; no demonstration is needed to see that DISTINCT collapses repeats.

practice_anchor.objective: Write a query that lists each distinct value of a category column (such as city in customers) exactly once.
practice_anchor.success: The query returns one row per distinct value, with no value repeated.

clusters.title: The Relational Model and SELECT Basics
clusters.reasoning: The relational model (tables, rows, columns, relationships) is the conceptual foundation for SQL, and SELECT is the first query that retrieves from it. A learner needs the model to understand what SELECT returns. These two concepts are the entry point to SQL and read as one idea: what a relational database is and how to query it.
